Introduction to the \(\SIR\) epidemic
=====================================
In a population of fixed size, 
an \(\SIR\) epidemic runs under the following stochastic dynamics:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{\emph{Infection: }} & &\text{transition }S\to S-1\,,\; I \to I+1 & \text{ occurs at rate }
    & \alpha \, S\, I\,,
\\
\text{\emph{Removal: }}   & &\text{transition }I\to I-1\,,\; R \to R+1 & \text{ occurs at rate }
    & \beta \, I\,.
\end{aligned}
\]
The structural parameter of epidemic `duration` 
(a positive real number)
and the `initial` configuration
(of `SIR` type) are given by
`julia` constants,
as are the per-pair infection rate `α` and the per-individual rate of removal `β`.
Population size is computed as part of the construction of `initial`, 
generating an extra
mark `n` obtained by computing the sum of 
the `s`, `i`, and `r` fields of the `SIR` constructor
(namely, the non-negative integers supplied by the last three parameters).
```{julia}
const duration = 2.0;
const α, β = 0.2, 1.5;
const initial = SIR(0.0, 5, 1, 0);
```

Structure of potential infections and removals
==============================================
The epidemic is defined by `initial` together with an `Innovation`
structure recording times of potential incidents,
using convenient single-letter abbreviations
(potential infections `I` or `ℐ`,
perpetuated infections `P` or `𝒫`,
potential removals `R` or `ℛ`
and conditioned removals `C` or `𝒞`),
```{julia}
A = AbstractInfection; I = Infection; P = PInfection; R = Removal; C = CRemoval;

innov1 = Innovation(initial.n,
    A[  I(0.11, 2, 3), I(0.2, 2, 5), P(0.4, 1, 2), I(0.5, 2, 5),  I(0.6, 2, 4), I(0.75, 1, 2), 
        I(0.85, 3, 4), I(0.9, 2, 3), I(1.0, 2, 5), I(1.05, 4, 5), I(1.1, 2, 3), P(1.2, 2, 4), 
        I(1.45, 4, 6), I(1.5, 3, 4),  I(1.6, 3, 5)  ],
    R[  R(0.3, 5), R(0.42, 3), R(0.7, 3), R(0.55, 3), R(0.95, 5), R(1.4, 2), R(1.55, 1),
        R(1.85, 2) ],
    C[  C(1.3, 2), C(0.8, 1), C(1.7, 4), C(1.8, 4), C(1.92, 5) ])
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Constructing the epidemic
An epidemic can now be constructed as follows;
the epidemic
`evol1 = Evolution(initial, innov1)`
starts at the `initial` state at process time \(0.0\) and then evolves
in process time 
based on the various potential incidents
held in the `Innovations`
structure `innov1`. 
@tbl-evolution tabulates the epidemic trajectory 
`evol1 = Evolution(initial, innov1)`
up to time `duration=2.0`
for initial state `initial` and a particular `Innovation` structure `innov1`.
```{julia}
#| label: tbl-evolution
#| tbl-cap: Evolution of an epidemic
#| echo: false 
evol1 = Evolution(initial, innov1)

flow = table_trajectories1(duration, evol1.trajectory) ;
header = [:t, :susceptibles, :infectives, :removals, :epidemic]
Markdown.parse(pretty_table(String, flow[:,header], 
  header=header, tf=tf_markdown, alignment=[:l, :c, :c, :c, :c]))
```



Plotting the epidemic
=====================
We need graphical visualizations of
simulation of the epidemic
conditional on all activated removals being observed
(denoting such activated removals by `C ⇒ 𝒞`
signifying "conditional removal");
with the ultimate objective of deriving a perfect simulation under this conditioning.
Note that the assumption of all activated removals being observed
is idealized, but not entirely unrealistic.

The epidemic curve
------------------
@fig-introduction-02-curves displays the epidemic curve together with 
trajectories of removals and susceptibles.
@fig-introduction-02-curves is also annotated at the two distinct epidemic curve peaks
of this particular simulation.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-introduction-02-curves
#| fig-cap: "Epidemic curve (with annotated peaks) together with monotonic \
#|           trajectories of numbers of susceptibles and removals. [`02-curves`]"
curves_template = plot(flow, yintercept=1:initial.n,
    Geom.hline(style=:dash, size=0.1mm, color=theme.scaffold),
    Coord.cartesian(xmin=0, xmax=duration, ymin=0, ymax=initial.n + 0.25),
    Guide.xlabel("Process time", orientation=:horizontal),
    style(default_color=theme.background),
    gadfly_theme) ;

push!(curves_template, layer(flow, x=:t, y=:empty, Geom.line,
    style(line_width=2theme.trail, default_color=theme.scaffold))) ;

incidents_template = new_figure(curves_template,
    Scale.y_continuous(labels=(initial.n ≤ EpidemicsUtilities.MAXPOP ?
        i -> EpidemicsUtilities.timelinelabels_circled(i; n=initial.n) :
        i -> EpidemicsUtilities.timelinelabels_bracketed(i; n=initial.n))),
    Guide.yticks(ticks=collect(1:(initial.n))),
    Guide.ylabel("Time lines")) ;

push!(curves_template,
    Scale.y_continuous(labels=(i -> EpidemicsUtilities.timelinelabel_raw(i; n=initial.n))),
    Guide.ylabel("Numbers of individuals")) ;

figure03 = new_figure(curves_template, 
    layer(flow, x=:t, y=:infectives, Geom.step,
        style(line_width=theme.boundary, default_color=theme.colour(I))),
    layer(flow, x=:t, y=:removals, Geom.step,
        style(line_style=[:dashdot], line_width=theme.boundary, default_color=theme.colour(R))),
    layer(flow[flow.susceptibles.!=0, :], x=:t, y=:susceptibles, Geom.step,
        style(line_style=[:dash], line_width=theme.boundary, default_color=theme.scaffold)),
) ;

depict("introduction-02-curves", new_figure(figure03,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        text(1.2, 3.2, "Peak #1"),
        text(1.6, 3.2, "Peak #2"),
        text(0.0, 5.1, "Susceptibles"),
        text(0.0, 1.1, "Infectives"),
        text(1.0, 1.1, "Removals"),
        fontsize(6pt))),
    title="Epidemic curve with removals and susceptibles"
    ))
```


Plotting zone boundaries
------------------------
For the coupling construction it is convenient to suppose the
various time lines are infected in increasing index order (because of a re-labelling symmetry,
the statistics of the
evolutions of total numbers of `susceptibles`, `infectives` and `removals` are not affected).
Thus the epidemic is now defined by boundaries between a _removals zone_ and
an _infectivity zone_, and between the infectivity zone and a _susceptible zone_.
@fig-introduction-03-boundary illustrates these boundaries.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-introduction-03-boundary
#| fig-cap: "Time-evolving boundaries between susceptible, infected,       \
#|           and removed sub-populations. Note that the boundary between   \
#|           susceptible and infected is itself infected; similarly the    \
#|           boundary between infected and removed (or between susceptible \
#|           and removed) is itself removed. [`03-boundary`]"
depict("introduction-03-boundary", 
    new_figure(
        draw_regions!(deepcopy(incidents_template), 
            duration, evol1, theme=theme, select=BOUNDARIES | TOP),
        title="Boundaries for the coupling construction")
)
```

Plotting infectivity and removed zones
--------------------------------------
Space-time zones of infection and removal
use a blend of the original data frame with lagged data
(@tbl-evolution-enhanced).
Actual zones of infectivity and removals (@fig-introduction-04-zones)
are closed at their upper boundaries: the top edge of
the infectivity zone is to be considered as _infected_
so long as this is not also the top of the removals zone, 
the top edge of the removals zone is to be considered as _removed_.
```{julia}
#| label: tbl-evolution-enhanced
#| tbl-cap: Enhanced table giving evolution of the epidemic
#| echo: false
xy_flow = table_trajectories2(flow, theme=theme) ;
Markdown.parse(pretty_table(String, xy_flow[:,header], 
  header=header, tf=tf_markdown, alignment=[:l, :c, :c, :c, :c]))
```
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-introduction-04-zones
#| fig-cap: "Infectivity and removal zones. [`04-zones`]"
figure_zones = draw_regions!(deepcopy(incidents_template), 
    duration, evol1, theme=theme, select=BOUNDARIES | REGIONS)
depict("introduction-04-zones", new_figure(figure_zones,
    title="Zones of infectivity and removal"))
```

Adding incidents to the plot
----------------------------
@fig-introduction-05-incidents adds incidents corresponding to the underlying `innov1`
using the `EpidemicsUtilities` function `draw_elements`. This figure
does not yet take account of whether or not incidents are activated,
but merely illustrates the occurrences of the various incidents..
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-introduction-05-incidents
#| fig-cap: "Incidents arising from the `innov1` structure,                   \
#|           together with the epidemic curve and infectivity and             \
#|           removal zones. Note that most of these incidents will turn out   \
#|           to be inactive. Zones are closed at upper edges: the upper       \
#|           boundary of the infectivity zone is \"infected\",                \
#|           whilst the upper boundary of the removal zone is \"removed\".    \
#|                                             [`05-incidents`]"
depict("introduction-05-incidents", new_figure(
    draw_evolution!(deepcopy(figure_zones), evol1, duration, theme=theme, select=ELEMENTS),
    title="Incidents driving the epidemic")
)
```


Indicating activated incidents
------------------------------
Only some of these incidents are actually activated by the construction:

 * _Infections_ (`I ⇒ ℐ` and `P ⇒ 𝒫`) must lie inside the infectivity zone with
 infectee marks reaching 
 up to the time line which at that point of time is immediately above
 the infectivity zone (and hence must reach exactly
 one time line above the highest infected time line);
 * _Removals_ (`R ⇒ ℛ` and `C ⇒ 𝒞`) must lie inside the infectivity zone.

This is illustrated in @fig-introduction-06-activated, where the activated incidents
are emphasized by being drawn using arrows with thicker lines.
Note that perpetuated infections (`P ⇒ 𝒫`) arise
as part of the evolution of the entire $\SIR$ trajectory in algorithmic time.
Note also that conditioned removals (`R ⇒ ℛ`)
are the _only_ removals which should be activated.
Were an ordinary removal
(`R ⇒ ℛ`) to be activated then this would break the imposed conditioning (of all
observed removals).

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-introduction-06-activated
#| fig-cap: "Activated incidents (thicker arrows) driving the epidemic:       \
#|           notice that activated removals are exactly those removals lying  \
#|           in the infectivity zone, while activated infections are exactly  \
#|           those infections reaching from within the infectivity zone to    \
#|           just above it. [`06-activated`]"
depict("introduction-06-activated", new_figure(
    draw_evolution!(deepcopy(figure_zones), evol1, duration, theme=theme, select=BASIC),
    title="Incidents driving the epidemic, emphasizing activated incidents")
)
```



Evolving the epidemic in algorithmic time
=========================================
We can now give a visual explanation of how to evolve
an $\SIR$ epidemic _in algorithmic time_,
subject to conditioning
on observed (conditioned) removals.
A single step of algorithmic time evolution can be broken down into a number of sub-steps:

1. Sample a new `Innovation` structure with fixed times for the conditional removals;
2. Remove all unconditioned removals
(those removals not activated, denoted by `R ⇒ ℛ`);
3. Insert precisely those removals from the new `Innovation` 
structure which will not be activated
(equivalently, which do not lie in the infectivity zone);
4. Re-sample proposed time lines for each of the conditioned removals
(denoted by `C ⇒ 𝒞`),
accepting proposals for which the relevant conditioned removal 
is still in the infectivity zone; 
5. Now work from right to left, deciding for each old infection incident from the new `Innovation`
whether it is to be removed, and for each new infection incident from the new `Innovation`
whether it is to be introduced:
   - an old infection incident is removed unless so doing 
 would result in a conditioned removal (`C ⇒ 𝒞`) _not_ being removed. 
 If that
 turns out to be the case, then the old infection incident is retained
 but converted into a _perpetuated_ infection (`P ⇒ 𝒫`);
   - a new infection incident is introduced unless so doing would
 result in a potential (but not activated / conditioned) removal (`R ⇒ ℛ`)
 being activated.
 If that
 turns out to be the case, then the new infection incident is not introduced.
 
There are two substantial issues:

A) we need to organize 
the calculations required for making the decisions in item 5;

B) we must show the algorithmic time evolution 
is "monotonic" in a way
that permits implementation of CFTP,


Sample a new `Innovation` structure
-----------------------------------
The first sub-step is to produce a randomly sampled innovation
`innov_candidate`
(using the function `generate_innovation`).
with conditioned removals
occurring at the same times but with randomly
assigned different `target` time lines.
Compare the original innovation `innov1` with `innov_candidate`: 
```{julia}
#| echo: false
println("innov1 = ", sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), innov1))
innov_candidate = generate_innovation(innov1, duration, α=α, β=β)
println("innov_candidate = ", sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), innov_candidate))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
# Explanatory note concerning `innov_candidate`
Note that `innov_candidate` is an independent innovation.
It is not used directly in defining a new `Evolution`, but is used
as a supply of components in what follows.
:::



It is not correct simply 
to replace `innov1` by `innov_candidate`, as this will break the conditioning
on observed removals.
Instead 
it is necessary to work systematically through
each
change in turn (removal of old incident, introduction of new incident,
replacing old by new conditioned removal mark), checking at each point to
check that the conditioning is not broken.

::: {.callout-warning}
# An important expositional point
Evidently some care has to be taken to insure that individual changes satisfy the requirements
of some kind of generalized detailed balance condition, in order to be assured that the changes
preserve the conditional distribution of the $\SIR$ epidemic. This should be discussed carefully 
in the paper now being drafted: it is one of the crucial steps of the entire argument!
:::

We insert some incidents in `innov_candidate`
to force some issues to arise in algorithm implementation:

a) an extra infection which might affect the \LFE infection;
```{julia}
push!(innov_candidate.infections, I(1.1, 2, 4), )
```
b) some extra infections which might produce a faster 
epidemic without hitting new removals;
```{julia}
push!(innov_candidate.infections, I(0.5, 1, 2), I(0.85, 2, 4), I(1.05, 2, 3), I(1.55, 4, 6))
```
c) a couple of inactivated removals in time lines 2 and 3 
which might affect the \NOFLYZONE;
```{julia}
push!(innov_candidate.removals, R(0.3, 2), R(0.1, 3))
```


Remove all inactive removals from previous `Innovation`
-------------------------------------------------------
We now sequentially deploy the incidents of `innov_candidate`, inserting selected 
kinds of incidents 
into successive modifications `innov1_x` (for `x=0, 1, ...`)
of the original `Innovation` `innov1`
so as to ensure that conditions on activated removals are not violated
when `innov1_x` is used to update `innov1` to produce `evol_x`.
First remove all unactivated removals from `innov1`: see @fig-introduction-07-old-removals-gone. 
```{julia}
innov1_0 = Innovation(initial.n, innov1.infections, R[], innov1.cremovals)
evol1_0 = Evolution(initial, innov1_0)
```
::: {.callout-tip}
# Explanatory note for `innov1_0`
This is obtained from `innov1` 
by omitting all (old) `inactive_removals`.

The resulting `Evolution` structure 
`evol1_0 = Evolution(initial, innov1_0)` 
therefore yields the same trajectory as `evol1 = Evolution(initial, innov1)`.
:::

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-introduction-07-old-removals-gone
#| fig-cap: "This is @fig-introduction-06-activated, but with all non-activated removals      \
#|           taken away, while retaining conditioned removals, as specified in `innov1_0`. \
#|           [`07-old-removals-gone`]"
depict("introduction-07-old-removals-gone", new_figure(
    draw_evolution!(deepcopy(figure_zones), evol1_0, duration, theme=theme, select=BASIC),
    title="The epidemic as before, deleting all non-activated removals")
)
```

Adding in those removals from the new innovation which remain inactive
----------------------------------------------------------------------
We now insert those of the removals from `innov_candidate` which 
would _not_ be activated by the old epidemic structure. 
To do this, we use the `Evolution` attributes `start_times` and `finis_times`,
holding "birth" and "death" times of the infection for each time line.
Note that we assume that _every_ time line dies at time `Inf` if
it is still alive at the time `duration`,
and is born at time `0.0` if it has not been infected by time `duration`: 
evidently this is unrealistic
but flags absence of data.

::: {.callout-warning}
It might be more logical to have default time line "birth" occurring at time `-Inf`?
:::

We now employ a function `EpidemicsCFTP.inactive_removals` which
returns a list composed of:

a) removals occurring before respective time line is infected (before relevant `start_time`);

b) removals occurring on or after respective time line is removed
(after relevant `finis_time`): these removals are all converted to `KilledRemoval`s.

This allows us to add the new inactive removals from `innov_candidate` to `innov1_0`,
converting those in the removals zone to `KilledRemoval`s, forming
a resulting (intermediate) evolution `innov1_1` which is
used to plot @fig-introduction-08-inactive-removals.
```{julia}
innov1_1 = Innovation(initial.n, innov1_0.infections, 
    EpidemicsCFTP.inactive_removals(evol1, innov_candidate), innov1_0.cremovals)
evol1_1 = Evolution(initial, innov1_1)
```
::: {.callout-tip}
# Explanatory note for `innov1_1`
This is obtained from `innov1_0` 
by using the `inactive_removals` method to insert all (non-conditional) removals
in `innov_candidate` which would not be activated by the trajectory of `evol1`
equivalently `evol1_0`. Removals in the removals zone 
are re-typed as `KilledRemoval`.

The resulting `Evolution` structure 
`evol1_1 = Evolution(initial, innov1_1)` 
actually yields the same trajectory as `evol1`
equivalently `evol1_0` (since no inserted removals will be activated).
:::

Re-sampling using proposed time lines for conditioned removals
--------------------------------------------------------------
Now consider the conditioned removals. Compare the old and new conditioned removals
and determine whether the old can be replaced by the corresponding new conditioned removal.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
Markdown.parse("""
| `CRemoval` source               | Resulting list of `CRemoval`s                             |
|:--------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| Old conditioned removals:       | `$(sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), innov1.cremovals))`   |
| Candidate conditioned removals: | `$(sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), innov1_1.cremovals))` |
""")
```
Replacement is permitted exactly if
the new conditioned removal is still activated.
This happens if it lies in the infectivity zone given by the corresponding
interval from `periods(evol1_1)`,
as determined by the function `EpidemicsCFTP.resulting_cremovals`.

@fig-introduction-09-processed-cremovals graphs the resulting evolution `evol1_2`:
```{julia}
innov1_2 = Innovation(initial.n, innov1_1.infections, 
                innov1_1.removals, 
                EpidemicsCFTP.resulting_cremovals(evol1_1, innov_candidate)) ;
evol1_2 = Evolution(initial, innov1_2) ;
```
::: {.callout-tip}
# Explanatory note for `innov1_2`
This is obtained from `innov1_1` 
by using `EpidemicsCFTP.resulting_cremovals`
to re-mark the `CRemoval`s.

Again the resulting `Evolution` structure 
`evol1_2 = Evolution(initial, innov1_2)` 
actually yields the same trajectory as `evol1`
equivalently `evol1_0` or `evol1_1`,
as marks are changed only if they do not de-activate the respective `CRemoval`,
hence do not affect the trajectory.
:::

```{julia}
#|           only the first onditioned removal (at time `t=0.80`) has actually had its mark   \
#|           changed (from `target=1` to `target=2`).                                         \

depict("introduction-09-processed-cremovals", new_figure(
    draw_evolution!(deepcopy(figure_zones), evol1_2, duration, theme=theme, select=BASIC),
    title="Marks for conditioned removals changed by accept/reject")
```

Removing old infection incidents and introducing new infection incidents where suitable
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
To carry out the next task we need to make some prior computations:

a) Compute the \LFE curve. 
We do this using new infections occurring _later_ than the previous epidemic curve
(working in reverse time);
but perpetuating active infections when there is nothing useful occurring later;
b) For each time line, compute the last inactive removal occurring prior to the
activated infection on that time line;
c) Now work through new infections occurring _earlier_ than the previous epidemic curve
(working in reverse time again)
but rejecting those which would lead to activation of a previously unactivated removal.

### The \LFE curve
Compare the active and inactive infections derived from the original `Evolution` structure
with those proposed by the new `Innovation` structure:
```{julia}
#| echo: false
println(
    rpad("old infections:", 20), 
        sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), evol1.infections),
    "\n",
    rpad("new infections:", 20), 
        sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), innov_candidate.infections)
)
```
@fig-introduction-10-with-all-new-infections displays
the infection incidents from `innov_candidate` 
superimposed on removals, active infections and epidemic and removal boundaries
from @fig-introduction-09-processed-cremovals.
Note that the new infection incidents have not yet been used to determine the 
new epidemic trajectory!
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-introduction-10-with-all-new-infections
#| fig-cap: "This displays _all_ the new infections from `innov_candidate`, (replacing     \
#|           all previous infections) together with re-marked conditional removals, new    \
#|           inactivated removals, and activated (but non-labelled) infections all derived \
#|           from @fig-introduction-09-processed-cremovals. Note that the new infections   \
#|           would _not_ produce the old epidemic (still displayed on the figure together  \
#|           with activated elements): indeed there is no guarantee that the new epidemic  \
#|           would even satisfy the removals conditioning! [`10-with-all-new-infections`]"
innov1_2a = Innovation(initial.n, 
    innov_candidate.infections, innov1_2.removals, innov1_2.cremovals) ;
evol1_2a  = Evolution(initial, innov1_2a) ;
evol1_2x  = CEvolution(initial, evol1_2.history) ;

figure10  = draw_innovation!(deepcopy(figure_zones), innov1_2a, theme=theme)

depict("introduction-10-with-all-new-infections", new_figure(
    draw_evolution!(figure10, evol1_2x, duration, theme=theme),
    title="New infections superimposed")
)
```

If an infection has `target` mark referring to a time line which is
"removed" at the infection time (mark `t`) then it can never be
activated and so is essentially irrelevant. We signal this by
replacing the infection by a `KilledInfection` using the following function.
(And similarly for removals.)
We can then distinguish visually between infections occurring before and after removal
(@fig-introduction-11-dividing-infections1).
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-introduction-11-dividing-infections1
#| fig-cap: "This improves on @fig-introduction-10-with-all-new-infections by converting to \
#|            `KilledInfection`s all `Infection`s occurring after removal for               \
#|           the relevant time line. `KilledInfection`s are displayed in light              \
#|           gray. Note again  that the new infections would _not_ produce the              \
#|           old epidemic (still displayed on the figure together with activated elements)  \
#|           `[introduction-11-dividing-infections1]`"
differentiated = EpidemicsCFTP.kill_irrelevant_infections(evol1_2, innov_candidate)
innov1_2b = Innovation(initial.n, differentiated, innov1_2.removals, innov1_2.cremovals) ;
figure11  = draw_innovation!(deepcopy(figure_zones), innov1_2b, theme=theme)
figure11  = draw_evolution!(figure11, evol1_2x, duration, theme=theme)

depict("introduction-11-dividing-infections1", new_figure(figure11,
    title="Distinguishing between new infections occurring before and after removal")
)
```

The \LFE is formed by the slowest possible chain of activatable infections from `evol1_2`,
together with new infections from `innov_candidate`,
that trigger all of the conditioned removals of `evol1_2`,
and this is achieved so long as the proposed chain triggers those 
conditional removals for which the `target` field delivers
an increase in the running supremum.
This observation helps us to consider which 
of the new infections _prior_ to removal
```{julia}
#| echo: false
[z for z in EpidemicsCFTP.kill_irrelevant_infections(evol1_2, innov_candidate) if 
    z isa OperativeInfection]
```
are relevant
to construction of the \LFE. 
For such an infection, the `target` mark must lie in the infectious
zone, and the `infectee` mark must not lie below the most recent running supremum.
The relevant infections are computing using the function `EpidemicsCFTP.relevant_infections`
and are depicted in @fig-introduction-12-with-relevant-infections.
Note that the displayed set of relevant infections
```{julia}
#| echo: false
EpidemicsCFTP.relevant_infections(evol1_2, innov_candidate)
```
includes some infections that will not be considered for the \LFE,
because their `target` marks are above the epidemic trajectory.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-introduction-12-with-relevant-infections
#| fig-cap: "This improves on @fig-introduction-11-dividing-infections1 by emphasizing the _relevant_ \
#|           _relevant_ infections from `innov_candidate` (those which are additionally relevant      \
#|            to the \"last feasible epidemic\", which are coloured in hot-pink outline with text).   \
#|           [`12-with-relevant-infections`]"
relevant = EpidemicsCFTP.relevant_infections(evol1_2, innov_candidate)
figure12 = new_figure(figure11,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
         draw_feasible_incident(relevant, 2, theme=theme))),
)
depict("introduction-12-with-relevant-infections", new_figure(figure12,
    title="Relevant new infections are emphasized")
)
```


We now compute the \LFE, namely
the trajectory of the _last_ possible epidemic path that activates
all the `CRemoval` events and none of the `Removal` events. 
This is most easily accomplished by computing
in reverse time.
We use the function `EpidemicsCFTP.last_feasible_evolution`.
It first computes a new `chronology` by mixing the relevant infections from `innov_candidate`,
the activated infections from `innov1_2`,
and the conditioned removals
and then computes the reverse-initial state as the final state of the evolution
(epidemic state at time `duration`).
By this means we can compute and display the trajectory and history of the \LFE using:
```{julia}
last_feasible_trajectory, last_feasible_history = 
    EpidemicsCFTP.last_feasible_evolution(duration, evol1_2, innov_candidate) ;

# Next list comprehension is required to make sure that the list type is correct!
last_feasible_new_infections = [z for z ∈ last_feasible_history ∩ innov_candidate.infections]
perpetuated_infections       = [PInfection(z) for z ∈ last_feasible_history ∩ evol1.infections]
flow_last_feasible           = table_trajectories1(duration, last_feasible_trajectory)
evol1_2y  = CEvolution(initial, evol1_2.history, LFE=last_feasible_trajectory)
```

and should be put in a function! Examine it in `VScode`.
OR REPLACE AS PER test.qmd.

```{julia}
    [z.t for z in last_feasible_history if z isa AbstractInfection], [duration])
LFE_levels = 
    collect((initial.r + initial.i):
    (initial.r + initial.i + length(LFE_times)-1))
LFE_levels[end] = initial.r + initial.i + length(LFE_times) - 2
    
LFE_flow = DataFrame(t=LFE_times, epidemic=LFE_levels)
```

The next step is to abandon even the activated infections from the previous `Evolution`
excepting only those which are required in the
last viable epidemic, and therefore have to be perpetuated (computed above as `perpetuated_infections`).

Computing the \NOFLYZONE
------------------------

::: {.callout-warning}
# EXPLORATORY FROM NOW ON
:::


We now determine the \NOFLYZONE.
This is done in stages:

(a) compute `max_removal_time`, a vector giving the times at which each time line becomes free of inactivated removals;
(b) compute `nofly_envelope0`, the monotonically increasing envelope of `nftz1`;
(c) compute `nofly_envelope`, a vector giving the times at which each time line starts to be available for infection
without hazard of causing activation of an inactivated removal.

Step (c) involves the use of the `relevant_infections`. 
It suffices to consider only those `relevant_infections` occurring _before_ the current epidemic,
since perpetuation has the effect of ensuring that `relevant_infections` occurring _after_ the current epidemic
cannot lead to epidemic trajectories rising above the current epidemic.

::: {.callout-warning}
# Prove we can restrict to early `relevant_infections`
We need to prove that perpetuation has the effect of ensuring that `relevant_infections`
cannot lead to epidemic trajectories rising above the current epidemic
if they occur _after_ the current epidemic.
:::

We begin with step (a).
```{julia}
early_inactivated_removals = 
    [z for z ∈ evol1_2.removals if z.t < evol1_2.finis_times[z.target]]
```
@fig-introduction-15-relevant-removals provides a visual check!

We now compute the time of last early inactivated removal for each time line, forming the vector `max_removal_time`.
```{julia}
max_removal_time = repeat([0.0], evol1_2.initial.n)
for z ∈ early_inactivated_removals
    max_removal_time[z.target] = max(max_removal_time[z.target], z.t)
end
```

::: {.callout-warning}
# Reminder re `max_removal_time`
Needs to be computed within `compute_nofly` function (below).
:::


Then we take step (b), and compute the monotonic envelope `nofly_envelope0` of `max_removal_time`.
```{julia}
nofly_envelope0 = accumulate(max, max_removal_time)
println(nofly_envelope0)
```
::: {.callout-warning}
# Reminder re `nofly_envelope0`
Needs to be computed within `compute_nofly` function (below).
:::



We now need to move on to step (c). We prepare for this by reducing the set of
`innov_candidate.infections` to the _current infections_,
with `target` lying in one of the susceptible or infectious zones.
```{julia}
current_infections = 
    sort([z for z ∈ innov_candidate.infections if 
                z.t < evol1_2.finis_times[z.target]], lt=isearlier)
```
Note here that the vectors `evol1_2.start_times` and `evol1_2.finis_times` are 
actually the vectors of infection and removal times for the original epidemic trajectory
(which up to this point is the trajectory generated using all the modified `innov1_x`
for `x=0..2`).
```{julia}
#| echo: false
print("Infection times : ") ; println(evol1_2.start_times)
print("Removal times   : ") ; println(evol1_2.finis_times)
```
Furthermore we must
focus only on those infections in `current_infections` which extend beyond the original epidemic trajectory.

::: {.callout-note}
# Exposition alert
We deal with the _trajectory_ of `evol1_2`, which is the original trajectory:
it needs careful explanation why we use this not some new trajectory.
It is justified because our basic plan is to renew
infections working backwards through time ...
:::

We further reduce to `posterior_relevant_infections`, those infections whose `infectee`
has already been already infected (and hence whose `infectee` will not yet be removed),
and `prior_relevant_infections`
(those infections whose `infectee` has **not** already been infected).
```{julia}
posterior_relevant_infections =  [z for z ∈ current_infections if 
                                    z.t ≥ evol1_2.start_times[z.infectee]]
prior_relevant_infections = setdiff(current_infections, posterior_relevant_infections)
println("Prior relevant infections:    \n", 
    sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), prior_relevant_infections))
println("Posterior relevant infections:\n", 
    sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), posterior_relevant_infections))
```

Needs to be computed within a function?

Now we perform a careful computation of the "true" boundary: we
work backwards through the `prior_relevant_infections` 
as explained by the annotations to the code below. 
```{julia}
function compute_nofly(ev, iv, early_inactivated_removals)
    initial = ev.initial
	envelope0 = repeat([0.0], initial.n)                                       # <1>
	for removal ∈ early_inactivated_removals  # ev.removals?                   # <1>
	    envelope0[removal.target] = max(envelope0[removal.target], removal.t)  # <1>
	end                                                                        # <1>
	envelope = accumulate(max, envelope0)                                      # <1>
	
	processed_infections = AbstractInfection[]                                 # <2>
	 
	for z ∈ reverse(sort(iv.infections, lt=isearlier))                         # <3>
	    
	    if (z.t ≥ ev.finis_times[z.target])                                    # <4>
	        push!(processed_infections, KilledInfection(z))                    # <4>
            # @info "$(KilledInfection(z))"
	        continue                                                           # <4>
	    end                                                                    # <4>
	    
	    # At this stage of the iteration 
	    # @assert(z.t < ev.finis_times[z.target])
	    #
        if (z.t ≥ envelope[z.infectee])                                        # <5>
	        push!(processed_infections, z)                                     # <5>
	        continue                                                           # <5>
	    end                                                                    # <5>
	    
	    # At this stage of the iteration 
	    # @assert(z.t < ev.finis_times[z.target])
	    # @assert(z.t < envelope[z.infectee])
	    #
        if (z.t < envelope[z.infectee - 1])                                    # <6>
	        push!(processed_infections, z)                                     # <6>
	        continue                                                           # <6>
	    end                                                                    # <6>
	    
	    # At this stage of the iteration 
	    # @assert(z.t < envelope[z.infectee])
	    # @assert(z.t ≥ envelope[z.infectee - 1])
	    # @assert(z.t < ev.finis_times[z.target])
	    #
	    if (z.t ≥ ev.start_times[z.target])                                    # <7>
            if (z.t < ev.start_times[z.infectee - 1])                          # <8>
                envelope[z.infectee - 1] = z.t                                 # <8>
                push!(processed_infections, NoFlyInfection(z))                 # <8>
                # @info "$(NoFlyInfection(z))"
                continue                                                       # <8>
            else                                                               # <8>
                push!(processed_infections, ExpungedInfection(z))              # <8>
                # @info "$(ExpungedInfection(z))"
                continue                                                       # <8>
            end                                                                # <8>
	    end
	    
	    # At this stage of the iteration 
	    # @assert(z.t < envelope[z.infectee])
	    # @assert(z.t ≥ envelope[z.infectee - 1])
	    # @assert(z.t < ev.start_times[z.target])
	    # 
	    envelope[z.infectee - 1] = z.t                                         # <9>
	    push!(processed_infections, NoFlyInfection(z))                         # <9>
        # @info "$(NoFlyInfection(z))"
	
	end
	
	flow_nofly = DataFrame(t=envelope, y=(1:initial.n).+1, top=(initial.n)+1)
	xy_flow_nofly = table_trajectories2(flow_nofly; theme=theme)
	deleteat!(xy_flow_nofly, [(2*initial.n)-1])
	
	return processed_infections, flow_nofly, xy_flow_nofly
end ;
```
1. Here is the initial computation of `envelope`, a **list of times** 
indexed by time line ("level"), where each time is initially defined as
the supremum of times of **inactivated** `Removal`s at given level or 
below. So the envelope increases monotonically with level.
2. The list `processed_infections` of processed `AbstractInfection`s will
eventually store (initially in reverse time order) a transformation of
each infection supplied by the new `Innovation` `innov`.
3. Iteration: work backwards through `Infection`s supplied by `innov`,
determining in each case how to transform the supplied `Infection`
when adding it to the list `processed_infections`.
4. If the `Infection` `z` has `target` on the removed portion of a level
then it will never be activated, so add `z` as a `KilledInfection`.
5. If the `Infection` `z` potentially infects a level at a _later time_ 
than the current `envelope` at that level, then its activation will
never break the conditioning (**needs proof!**), so add `z` as-is.
(I think the point is: since we are working backwards in time, once
`z.t` is considered then `envelope` is frozen from time `t` onwards.)
6. However if `z.t < envelope[z.infectee - 1]` then no issue can arise, as 
infection of the level immediately below `z.infectee` will then not be
allowed at this time. So again add `z` as-is.
7. Suppose `z.t ≥ ev.start_times[z.target]`: then an issue would arise
if the level at `z.infectee - 1` were to become infected before
`z.t`. One of two cases must hold:
8. Case (a): Suppose `z.t < ev.start_times[z.infectee - 1]`.
Then **increase** `envelope[z.infectee - 1]` to `z.t` in order to
preclude the time line getting infected, and also transform `z` to a
`NoFlyInfection` when added to `processed_infections`, to signal
that it should never become infected.  
Case (b): Suppose `z.t ≥ ev.start_times[z.infectee - 1]`.
Then increasing `envelope[z.infectee - 1]` to `z.t` would lead to a
problem, since this level is infected at time `z.t`. Therefore we
transform `z` to a `ExpungedInfection` when we add it to 
`processed_infections`, so that it is treated as an
`InoperativeInfection`.
9. Consider now that potential `Infection`s to be treated later in this
iteration must have time mark earlier than `z.t`. If one of these were
to infect the level `z.infectee - 1` then it would follow by monotonicity
that the `z.target` level would become infected by that time `z.t`; and 
thus would create an infection of the `z.infectee` level at time `z.t`. 
In order for this to be prevented, we need to extend the `envelope` 
at level `z.infectee - 1` up to time `z.t`. We also transform `z`
to a `NoFlyInfection` when we add it to `processed_infections`, to
signal that it should never become infected.




```{julia}
#| echo: false
header = [:t, :y]
processed_infections, flow_nofly1, xy_flow_nofly1 = 
    compute_nofly(evol1_2, innov_candidate, early_inactivated_removals) ;
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
xy_flow_last_feasible = table_trajectories2(flow_last_feasible; theme=theme, forward=false) ;
```

Now compute the new innovation and evolution.
```{julia}
innov2 = Innovation(initial.n, 
                sort(processed_infections ∪ perpetuated_infections, lt=isearlier), 
                early_inactivated_removals, 
                evol1_2.cremovals) ;
evol2  = Evolution(initial, innov2) ; 
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-introduction-17-no-fly-zone
#| fig-cap: "Third (final) iteration of \"no-fly zone\", removing potential infections       \
#|           which would infect \"no-fly zone\" and illustrating trajectory and zones (by    \
#|           shading) of the last feasible epidemic. [`17-no-fly-zone`]"  
figure17 = new_figure(
    draw_evolution!(deepcopy(figure_zones), evol2, duration, theme=theme, select=ELEMENTS),
    
    # Draw activated incidents from last feasible epidemic (derived from previous
    # `evolution`!), without inscriptions.
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
       draw_activated_elements(initial, last_feasible_history, theme=theme))),

    # Draw, for each time line, nofly boundaries determined by running maximum calculation.
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        line([ [(0.0, z[1]), (z[2], z[1])] for z ∈ enumerate(max_removal_time) if z[2]>0]),
        linewidth(theme.boundary), stroke(theme.forbid1))),
        
    # Draw, for each time line, nofly boundaries determined by latest `Removal`.
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        line([ [(0.0, z[1]), (z[2], z[1])] for z ∈ enumerate(nofly_envelope0) if z[2]>0]),
        linewidth(theme.boundary), stroke(theme.forbid2))),
    
    # Draw Nofly region and boundary
    layer(flow_nofly1, x=:t, y=:y,  Geom.step(direction=:hv),
        style(line_width=theme.trail, default_color=theme.forbid2)),
    layer(xy_flow_nofly1, x=:t, ymin=:y, ymax=:top, Geom.ribbon,
        alpha=[theme.opacity], style(default_color=theme.forbid1)),

    # Draw Last Feasible Epidemic region and boundary
    layer(flow_last_feasible, x=:t, y=:epidemic, Geom.step(direction=:vh), 
        style(line_width=theme.dormant, default_color=theme.lastfeasible2)),
    layer(xy_flow_last_feasible, x=:t, ymin=:removals, ymax=:epidemic, Geom.ribbon,
        #alpha=[theme.opacity], 
        style(default_color=theme.lastfeasible1)),
    ) ;

depict("introduction-17-no-fly-zone", new_figure(figure17,
    title="Third (final) rendering of no-fly zone")
)
```


Now it remains to add the computation of the _new_ epidemic evolution.
We need the new flow.

```{julia}
flow = table_trajectories1(duration, evol2.trajectory) ;
xy_flow = table_trajectories2(flow, theme=theme) ;
```
